name: Erik Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, I'm 27, and I supervise the production planning office at a big building materials company. We make cement and concrete blocks at the works on the edge of town, and my dad worked in the kiln there for thirty years. I'm engaged to Clara, who's a receptionist at the dentist on Church Street, and we're getting married next June at our parish church. Most of our savings went on the deposits for the hall and the photographer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My team of five works out what the plant makes each week, which orders go out first, and when the kilns go down for maintenance. I spend a lot of my day walking between the office and the plant, because you can't plan a kiln shutdown from a desk. I like the people and the sense that what we make actually holds up houses. What wears me out is head office sending new targets every quarter, written by people who've never seen the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people got carried away with it. At work I'd say what I always say: the plant runs on people who know it. I don't post things online, but I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still have the usual worries. The wedding is costing more than we planned, and my pay is on the low side for a supervisor. There's nothing else like my job in this town except the plant itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the way I do now, and keep my head down until the wedding's paid for. I'd do a bit of overtime on shutdown weekends, which pays time and a half. And we'd cut the wedding guest list a bit, sorry to some cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit stretched. Nothing frightening, just tight money and a big year ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill worries you most this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The final payment on the hall in March. It's eighteen hundred, and we've got about half. My fiancée Clara's mum offered to help with the wedding, and I'd rather not, but we may have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any routine work on your team get automated even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the weekly order reports, which take Gary most of Monday. If a program did those, Gary would have more time on the plant floor, which is better. I wouldn't be worried for Gary's job, more for the reports being wrong.

say: People **got carried away** with AI, and I'd say so at the pub.
The plant runs on **people who know it**, not on computer programs.
think: My worries are the **wedding** costs and low supervisor pay.
There's **nothing else** like my job in this town except the plant.
do: Keep my **head down** until the wedding is paid for.
Work **overtime** on shutdown weekends at time and a half.
feel: **Steady** but stretched, with tight money and a big year ahead.
S0.quote: My fiancée Clara's mum offered to help with the wedding, and I'd rather not, but we may have to.
fieldNote: His pressures are **the wedding** and a one-employer town.
He'd **resist family help** but expects to take it.
His pride is in the **plant floor**, not the office.

steps.text: Keep running the planning office the same way
Work overtime on kiln shutdown weekends
Cut the wedding guest list to save on the hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tech firms selling bosses a shortcut, and a plant isn't a shortcut. At work I'd argue that planning needs people who know the kilns. I'd say young people should be doing apprenticeships, not courses on computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, planning is right there on that card. Head office would love to plan our week from a computer in the city. My team of five could become two, and I'd be lucky to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant manager about moving onto the maintenance side as an apprentice fitter. It'd mean a pay cut for a couple of years, but it's hands-on and slower to change. I wouldn't touch the AI planning tool unless I was told to, and then only the bare minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit angry. I don't like being told what's progress by people who never come here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a pay cut. Can you afford that before the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. I'd wait until after June, then apply. Clara's job is steady, and we'd live small for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's 58 and has done planning for twenty years. Gary is too old to start an apprenticeship and too young to retire. I'd fight for Gary before I'd fight for me.

say: Tech firms are **selling bosses a shortcut**, and a plant isn't a shortcut.
Young people need **apprenticeships**, not courses on computers.
think: **Planning** is on the card, and head office would do it remotely.
My team of five could **become two**.
do: Ask about an **apprentice fitter** role after the wedding.
Use the **AI planning tool** only when told to.
Live **small** for two years on reduced pay.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **angry** at outsiders defining progress.
S1.quote: Gary is too old to start an apprenticeship and too young to retire.
fieldNote: He moves toward **hands-on work** at the plant he grew up around.
He'd fight for a **long-serving colleague** before himself.

steps.text: Apply for an apprentice fitter role after the June wedding
Use the AI planning tool only when management requires it
Live on a tight budget for two years of apprentice pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, and people in power let it happen. I'd vote for whoever promises to protect working towns. I'd say it at church and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my office job is gone fast. Planning is thinking work, and AGI would do it from head office or from nowhere. The plant floor would last until the robots around 2031, so the fitters and the kiln crews outlast me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto the plant floor right away, even as a labourer if that's all there was. I'd make the wedding smaller, maybe just family and the church hall. And we'd lean on Clara's parents and mine if things got really bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, though I'd keep it to myself. Two years is no time at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd still marry in June. It'd just be smaller, and that's fine, that's what matters. Clara agrees, I asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think, picturing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say get on the floor and learn a trade, and he'd be right. He'd also say the plant has outlasted three owners. I'm not sure it outlasts robots.

say: It's **reckless**, and the people in power let it happen.
I'd vote for whoever promises to **protect working towns**.
think: My **office job** goes fast, because planning is pure thinking work.
The **plant floor** outlasts me until robots arrive, around 2031.
do: Move to the **plant floor** right away, even as a labourer.
Shrink the **wedding** to family and the church hall.
Lean on **both families** if things got bad.
S2.quote: My dad would say get on the floor and learn a trade, and he'd be right.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to move onto the plant floor.
He'd keep the **wedding date** but cut its size.

steps.text: Take any plant floor job, even as a labourer
Hold the wedding with just family in the church hall
Ask both sets of parents for help if pay stops
Vote for candidates who promise to protect working towns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train real tradespeople if we start now. I'd push the company to take on more apprentices. I'd say it to the plant manager and anyone else who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see my office job ending by 2031. I'd want to be a qualified fitter by then, which takes about three years. That gives me until about 2034 on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the wedding, I'd start the fitter apprenticeship and live on less. I'd try to save a bit, maybe fifty a month, but honestly the pay cut makes that hard. We'd wait on children until I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit sad. I liked my office job, but I'd make my peace with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Waiting on children is a big change. How does Clara feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clara wants children soon, and so do I. But I'd rather be qualified first than have a baby on apprentice pay. We'd talk and pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want the government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund apprenticeships properly, not handouts. Pay firms to train people like me. I don't want a cheque, I want a trade.

say: Five years is enough to **train tradespeople** if we start now.
The company should take on **more apprentices**.
think: My office planning job **ends by 2031**, whatever I do.
A **qualified fitter** has until about 2034 on the plant floor.
do: Start the **fitter apprenticeship** after the wedding.
Save about **fifty a month** despite the pay cut.
feel: **Worried and sad**, but making peace with it.
S3.quote: I don't want a cheque, I want a trade.
fieldNote: Delaying **children** is the cost he struggles with most.
His **faith** shapes how he'd decide with Clara.
He frames the government's role as **paying for training**, not income support.

steps.text: Start the plant's fitter apprenticeship after the wedding
Save fifty a month on apprentice pay
Wait to have children until he's qualified as a fitter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do things properly, the old way, with training. I'd want the town to plan for the plant changing. I'd say it at the parish council if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could stay in the office a few more years. But I'd still want to be on the floor by the early 2030s. I'd be 37 when AGI comes, hopefully with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in planning until about 2030, then do the fitter apprenticeship. We'd start a family after the wedding as planned. I'd save more once Clara's back at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but steadier. Ten years feels like a working life, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust the company to look after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. The plant manager is a decent man. Head office I don't trust at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young lad starting at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, learn the machines, and don't get stuck behind a desk. My dad told me that, and I didn't listen.

say: Ten years means doing things **properly**, the old way, with training.
The town should **plan** for the plant changing, starting at the parish council.
think: I could stay **in the office** a few more years.
I want to be **on the floor** by the early 2030s.
do: Start a **family** after the wedding as planned.
feel: **Uneasy but steadier**, like a working life, not a cliff.
S4.quote: Learn a trade, learn the machines, and don't get stuck behind a desk. My dad told me that, and I didn't listen.
fieldNote: He trusts the **local plant manager** but not head office.
Ten years lets him keep **family plans** on track.
He regrets not following his **dad's advice** earlier.

steps.text: Stay in the planning office until about 2030
Start the plant's fitter apprenticeship around 2030
Start a family with Clara after the June wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my office job goes and the wedding's just happened. What would help is apprenticeships for people my age, properly paid, so I could learn a trade at the plant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about towns like mine with one big employer. When the plant changes, the whole town changes with it.

headlineQuote: When the plant changes, the whole town changes with it.
portrait: Erik is 27 and supervises **production planning** at a cement and block works where his dad worked.
He's engaged to Clara, and **wedding costs** have drained their small savings.
He never uses AI and blames **tech firms** and head office for pushing it.
His plan in each picture is a **fitter apprenticeship** on the plant floor.
He wants **training, not handouts**, and leans on family and church.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his office job goes just after the wedding.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid **apprenticeships** for people his age.
